summary: For the Random Forest classifier, addressing class imbalance (class_weight='balanced', random oversampling, or SMOTE) did NOT improve overall model quality: macro-F1 was highest for the untouched baseline (0.800) and slightly lower for every imbalance-handling variant (0.788-0.798), and ROC-AUC/PR-AUC were also marginally worse. What imbalance handling does deliver is a large jump in balanced accuracy (0.778 -> 0.83) and minority-class (>50K) recall (0.61 -> ~0.81-0.84), but this comes at the cost of overall accuracy and precision, so the net effect on a balanced quality metric like macro-F1 is negative on this dataset's only moderate (~76/24) imbalance.
direction: baseline > class_weight=balanced (macro-F1 slightly decreases; ROC-AUC also slightly decreases; balanced accuracy and minority recall increase substantially)
methodological_choices: Dropped `fnlwgt` (census sampling weight, not an individual predictor) and `education` (redundant with ordinal `education-num`). Missing categoricals imputed as an explicit 'Missing' level rather than dropped (~7% of rows affected). One-hot encoding for categoricals, standard scaling for numerics (fit on train only, no leakage). Single stratified 70/30 train/test split for the primary comparison, random_state=42. Compared 4 imbalance-handling strategies (none/baseline, class_weight='balanced', random oversampling, SMOTE -- resampling applied to the training fold only) crossed with 2 model classes (Logistic Regression, Random Forest with 300 trees, min_samples_leaf=2). Random Forest with class_weight='balanced' used as the primary comparison since RF was the stronger base model on every metric and class_weight is the simplest/most standard imbalance intervention (no synthetic or duplicated rows). Chose macro-F1 (unweighted average of per-class F1) as the primary 'quality' metric, ahead of plain accuracy (biased toward the majority class) or ROC-AUC/PR-AUC (threshold-free, so mechanically less sensitive to a technique whose main effect is shifting the decision boundary/threshold trade-off); macro-F1, balanced accuracy, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, and minority-class precision/recall/F1 were all computed so the full trade-off is visible rather than picking a metric that flatters one side.
verification_method: (1) 5x repeated stratified 5-fold CV (5 different seeds via RepeatedStratifiedKFold, 25 folds total) comparing RF baseline vs RF class_weight='balanced' macro-F1 on each fold. (2) Bootstrap (2000 resamples) 95% CI on the macro-F1 difference (balanced - baseline) computed on the held-out test set's fixed predictions.
verification_result: Finding held up and was highly consistent: in the 5x5 repeated CV, macro-F1 was LOWER with class_weight='balanced' than baseline in all 25/25 folds (mean diff = -0.0121, std = 0.0047, range [-0.0264, -0.0027]). The bootstrap 95% CI on the test-set macro-F1 difference was [-0.0208, -0.0044], entirely below zero, confirming the decrease is not noise. So the initial (single-split) result that imbalance handling slightly hurts macro-F1 for this dataset/model was corroborated, not overturned, by both stability checks; note this is metric-dependent, since balanced accuracy and minority recall improved substantially under the same comparison.
